facts.text: I investigated two types of bubble detachment cases in a cooling plate.
In case one, the upper wall of the cooling plate was placed with a positive electrode.
In case one, the lower wall of the cooling plate was connected to ground.
In case one, a dielectric layer was coated at the lower wall of the cooling plate as an insulation layer.
In the simulation of case one, an air bubble of diameter 4 mm was surrounded by liquid water and initially attached to the wall of the cooling plate.
In case one, the initial contact angle of the bubble on the wall was set to 90°.
In case one, the electrodes were a pair of parallel discs at the bottom and top of the region.
In case one, the lower disc was connected to ground.
In case one, the voltage applied on the upper disc was a function of time.
In case one, the voltage was 0 for t in [0,1] s.
In case one, the voltage was 600t for t in [1,2] s.
In case one, the region size was 10 × 10 mm with a mesh number of 100 × 100.
In case one, the thickness of the dielectric layer was 0.1 mm.
In case one, the center of the bubble was located at (5, 0.1) mm.
In case one, a no-slip boundary condition was specified at two discs.
In case one, liquid water and air were assumed to be incompressible and perfectly dielectric.
In case one, from t=0 to 1 s the electric field did not apply to the region and the contact angle reached 103°.
In case one, at about t=1.43 s the bubble began to split up.
In case one, until t=1.46 s the contact angle had been saturated.
In case one, at t=1.43 s the disk electrode applied a voltage of 258 V at the top of the region.
In case one, at t=1.43 s the voltage drop mainly happened inside the bubble and dielectric layer.
In case one, the electric body force mainly acted on the two sides of the bubble to squeeze it to detach the surface.
In case one, the electrophoretic force was identified as the main factor causing bubble detachment when considering the triple contact point.
In case one, the largest electrophoretic force arrows acted on the triple contact point.
In case one, the dielectrophoretic force mainly acted on the dielectric layer contacting with water.
In case one, the electrostrictive force acted on the whole dielectric layer contacting with air and water.
In case two, the positive electrode was placed at another location.
In case two, the voltage was applied at the top of the bubble using an electrode with a length of 0.04 cm.
In case two, the voltage was 0 for t in [0,1] s.
In case two, the voltage was 800t for t in [1,2] s.
In case two, an air bubble attached below the rod electrode was considered.
In case two, the lower wall was connected to ground.
In case two, at t=1 s the bubble reached a contact angle of 103° when the electric field did not apply.
In case two, from t=1 s to t=2.58 s the apparent contact angle did not change because the electric body force was not large enough to split up the bubble.
In case two, at about t=2.59 s the bubble began to split up.
In case two, until t=2.80 s the contact angle had been saturated.
In case two, at t=2.59 s the electrode applied a voltage of 1270 V.
In case two, at t=2.59 s the voltage on the bubble was about 600 V.
In case two, at t=2.59 s the contact angle changed from hydrophobic to hydrophilic but the bubble encountered an unstable state due to non-uniform electric charge distribution.
In case one, the split-up voltage was 258 V at t=1.43 s.
In case one, the contact angle changed directly from hydrophobic to hydrophilic at bubble split-up.
In case one, the sudden disturbance of contact angle change caused a capillary wave that propagated from the bottom to the top of the bubble.
In case one, the radial curvature at the base became higher than the radial curvature at the top of the bubble.
In case one, the corresponding buoyancy force lifted the bubble away from the surface.
In case two, as the voltage at the liquid-vapor interface increased to 600 V the bubble began to split up.
In case two, as the voltage increased from 0 to 600 V the contact angle maintained hydrophobic.

In the study, a numerical model was developed using the VOF level set method for tracking the free surface with an electric body force model including electrophoretic, dielectrophoretic, and electrostrictive effects.
The electrodynamic model for charge density was proposed from Maxwell’s equations by neglecting magnetic induction.
If excitations were constant in time, the electrodynamic model could be simplified to an electrostatic model.
The numerical model results were verified with published experimental data.
The findings were stated to benefit the design of EV battery cooling plates.
The study examined two locations to place the electrode inside an EV battery cooling plate.
The study investigated the effects of voltage duration, voltage amplitude, and bubble dynamics on the split-up process.
In the simulation, the voltage used was a linear function of time.
In the parallel-disc electrode setup, the voltage on the liquid-vapor interface was 258 V to split up the bubble.
In the rod-electrode case, the voltage at the liquid-vapor interface increased to 600 V before the bubble began to split up.
The electrophoretic force was found to play an important role when considering the triple contact point.
Contact angle hysteresis was considered in the numerical simulation model.
Young-Lippmann’s equation was described as assuming contact angle changes with increased voltage under small errors associated with uniform-surface-charge.
The study used dielectric electrophoresis force to express inhomogeneity or spatial change of dielectric constant caused by non-uniform electric field, temperature gradient, and phase difference.
